name: Cracked Skin
preview_text: When your skin cracks and itches, TCM looks beyond moisturizers to the blood that feeds it - by nourishing Blood and dispelling Wind, many stubborn cases see lasting improvement wi...
synonyms: ["Skin Cracking", "Chapped Skin", "Skin Fissures", "Cracked or Peeling Skin on Hands and Feet"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, cracked skin (also called skin fissures) occurs when the outer layer of skin loses moisture and becomes dry, thickened, and inflexible. Common triggers include cold, dry weather, frequent hand washing, harsh soaps, or underlying skin conditions like eczema, psoriasis, and athlete's foot. Cracks can be painful, bleed, and increase the risk of infection. Diagnosis is usually based on appearance and history, sometimes with patch testing or blood work to rule out allergies or systemic diseases.
conventional_treatments: Standard care focuses on restoring the skin barrier: thick moisturizers, ointments, and barrier creams to lock in moisture. Topical corticosteroids may be prescribed to reduce inflammation and itching, while antifungal or antibiotic creams are used if an infection is present. For chronic conditions like eczema, doctors may recommend avoiding irritants, using gentle cleansers, and sometimes oral medications or light therapy.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the skin is an extension of the body's internal organs, and its moisture and flexibility depend on the smooth flow of Qi and the nourishing power of Blood and Body Fluids. When these internal resources run low, the skin becomes dry, brittle, and prone to splitting - much like a riverbed cracks when the water dries up.
The most common pattern behind chronic cracked skin is Blood Deficiency with External Wind. Imagine the skin as a field: if the soil (Blood) is depleted, the surface dries out and can no longer anchor itself. A dry Wind then sweeps across this weakened field, stripping away remaining moisture and causing the characteristic itching and flaking.
This is why cracks often worsen in dry, windy weather or after a long illness that has drained the body's reserves.
But not all cracking comes from deficiency. Sometimes toxic Heat from harsh chemicals, medications, or an acute skin inflammation attacks the skin directly, causing redness, swelling, and painful fissures that burn. In other cases, Cold invades the channels and joints, congealing Blood flow so that the skin loses its warmth and elasticity, leading to cracks that feel better with heat and worse in the cold.
And when the Spleen is too weak to produce enough Blood from food, the skin becomes pale, dry, and cracks without any redness or heat - a sign that the body's entire nourishing system is underpowered.
This is why one person's cracked heels respond to blood-nourishing herbs while another's need cooling, detoxifying formulas. By reading the tongue, pulse, and the story of the cracks - when they started, what makes them better or worse - a TCM practitioner identifies the root pattern and treats from the inside out.
classical_quote: 「血虚风燥，肌肤失养，故令皴裂。」
classical_translation: "When blood is deficient and wind-dryness prevails, the skin loses its nourishment, hence causing chapping and cracking."
classical_source:
Zhu Bing Yuan Hou Lun (Treatise on the Causes and Symptoms of Diseases)  ,  Volume 35, Chapter on Chapped Skin (皴裂疮候) 									·

tcm_diagnosis:
A practitioner first looks at how long the cracking has been present and what it feels like. If the skin has been dry, scaly, and itchy for a long time and the cracks appear gradually, it often points to Blood Deficiency with External Wind. The tongue is typically pale with a thin white coating, and the pulse feels thin and wiry.
In contrast, if the cracking came on suddenly with redness, swelling, and a burning pain, the practitioner suspects Toxic-Heat. This pattern often follows exposure to harsh chemicals, medications, or an acute skin inflammation. The tongue body is red with a yellow coating, and the pulse is rapid and possibly wiry.
When cracks are accompanied by a cold, aching pain and the skin looks darker or purplish, Cold invading the Channels is a strong possibility. This pattern worsens in cold weather and improves with warmth. The tongue may be pale or have a dusky color, and the pulse feels deep and slow.
If the person also feels tired, has a poor appetite, and notices their tongue is pale and puffy with teeth marks on the sides, Spleen Blood Deficiency may be the root cause. The cracks are often widespread and accompanied by general dryness. The pulse is weak and thready, reflecting a digestive weakness that fails to produce enough blood to moisturize the skin.

patterns.symptoms: ["Skin cracks and fissures that are dry, not weepy", "Itching that comes and goes or shifts location", "Worse at night and in dry, windy weather", "Pale or sallow complexion", "Aversion to wind or drafts", "Dizziness or light-headedness"]
patterns.worse_with: Dry, windy weather, Overwork and exhaustion, Poor nutrition, Hot, long showers, Stress and anxiety
patterns.better_with: Regular moisturizing, Warm, humid environment, Rest and adequate sleep, Gentle exercise
patterns.why_this_happens: When the body does not have enough nourishing Blood, the skin loses its natural moisture and flexibility. This underlying dryness makes the skin fragile and prone to tiny cracks. External Wind then invades this weakened surface, further stripping moisture and causing the classic itching, flaking, and deep fissures.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white and slightly dry coat. Pulse: fine (thin) and may feel wiry or floating.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood is the body's moisture; when it is deficient, the skin dries and cracks. External Wind then enters the dry, open surface, causing itching. Moisturizing and warm, humid air compensate for the lack of internal moisture, while rest and nourishing foods help rebuild Blood. Windy, dry weather and overwork further deplete Blood and invite Wind, making symptoms worse.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Apply a rich, fragrance-free moisturizer immediately after bathing to lock in hydration. Eat blood-building foods like dark leafy greens, black sesame seeds, and moderate amounts of red meat or bone broth. Shield your skin from cold wind with gloves and scarves, and avoid long, hot showers that strip natural oils.

patterns.why_this_happens: When strong external irritants, chemicals, or medications introduce Heat-toxin into the body, the toxin can rise to the skin. The toxic Heat damages the skin's integrity, causing redness, swelling, and painful cracking, often with a burning sensation. The Heat also consumes body fluids, leaving the skin dry and prone to deep fissures, and may even lead to pus formation.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body with prickly thorns, dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shǔ) and forceful (有力 yǒu lì), often full (实 shí) or overflowing (洪 hóng).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Toxic-Heat is an excess Hot condition; anything that adds Heat (spicy food, alcohol, hot weather) fuels the fire and worsens redness, swelling, and cracking. Cooling and detoxifying measures help clear the toxin, cool the blood, and allow the skin to heal. Emotional stress generates internal Heat, so staying calm is also protective.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, and deep-fried foods that add Heat. Eat cooling, moistening foods like cucumber, watermelon, mung beans, and pears. Drink plenty of water and protect skin from harsh chemicals and irritants.

patterns.why_this_happens:
Cold invades the channels and joints, causing Qi and Blood to contract and stagnate. This impairs the nourishment reaching the skin, leaving it dry, brittle, and prone to painful fissures. The skin often feels cold and may turn dark or purplish because the blood is not flowing freely.
The pain is fixed and intense, much like a frozen pipe that cracks under pressure, and it reliably worsens in cold environments while easing with warmth.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale body, thin white coat, moist surface. Pulse: tight (Jin), often wiry (Xian) and slow (Chi).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Cold contracts and congeals Qi and Blood, worsening the stagnation that starves the skin. Warmth relaxes the channels, encourages circulation, and delivers the nourishment needed to heal cracks. Warming foods and gentle movement stoke the body's internal Yang Qi, helping to drive out deep Cold and restore supple, intact skin.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Keep the affected skin warm and protected from drafts. Soak in warm water with a few slices of fresh ginger, then gently pat dry and apply a nourishing balm. Eat warming, cooked foods such as lamb stew with cinnamon and ginger, and avoid raw, cold foods and icy drinks.

patterns.why_this_happens: The Spleen is the main organ that produces Blood from the food we eat. When it becomes weak, it cannot make enough Blood to nourish the skin. The skin loses its natural moisture and elasticity, becoming dry, pale, and prone to cracking without any redness or heat.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, possibly thin body with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (thin), choppy, and weak at the right Guan position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: The Spleen produces Blood from the food we eat. Warm, cooked foods and regular meals support this process, while raw, cold, or greasy foods strain the Spleen and impair blood production. Rest and gentle movement conserve Qi, whereas overwork and stress deplete Spleen Qi. Nourishing the Spleen and Blood restores the skin's natural moisture and resilience, allowing cracks to heal.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Eat warm, cooked foods like soups, stews, and congees to support the Spleen. Include blood-nourishing ingredients such as red dates, goji berries, black sesame, and small amounts of liver. Avoid raw, cold, and greasy foods that weaken the Spleen. Eat regular meals and avoid overworking or skipping meals. Gentle exercise like walking or tai chi helps Qi and Blood circulation without depleting energy.

faqs.question: Why does my skin crack only in winter?
faqs.answer: Winter brings two challenges from a TCM perspective: external cold and internal dryness. Cold causes the channels to contract, slowing blood flow to the skin and leaving it undernourished. At the same time, indoor heating and cold winds strip moisture from the surface. If you already have an underlying Blood Deficiency, your skin has little reserve to withstand this double attack, and cracks appear. Warming, blood-nourishing herbs and protecting the skin from cold are key.

faqs.question: Can TCM help with cracked heels?
faqs.answer: Yes, cracked heels are often a classic sign of Blood Deficiency or Cold invading the lower body. When nourishing Blood fails to reach the extremities, the thick skin on the heels dries out and fissures under pressure. TCM treats this with internal herbs that build Blood and improve circulation, often combined with external soaks. Many patients notice the cracks begin to close and the skin becomes softer within a few weeks.

faqs.question: Will I need to take herbs forever?
faqs.answer: No. TCM herbal treatment for cracked skin is time-limited. Once the internal imbalance is corrected and the skin has healed, formulas are gradually reduced and then stopped. Some people with longstanding deficiencies may benefit from periodic tune-ups, but the goal is always to restore your body's own ability to nourish the skin, not to create dependency.

faqs.question: Can I use my regular moisturizer while taking TCM herbs?
faqs.answer: Absolutely. In fact, gentle, fragrance-free moisturizers work well alongside TCM treatment. The herbs address the root cause from the inside while the moisturizer protects the skin barrier externally. Just avoid products with harsh chemicals or strong fragrances that could further irritate cracked skin.

faqs.question: Is acupuncture painful for cracked skin?
faqs.answer: Acupuncture uses hair-thin needles and most people feel only a tiny pinch or a mild sensation of warmth or heaviness. For skin cracking, the needles are typically placed on the limbs, abdomen, or back - not directly into the cracks themselves - so the treatment is comfortable. Many patients find sessions deeply relaxing.

faqs.question: How quickly will I see results?
faqs.answer: That depends on your pattern. Acute cracks from a chemical irritant (Toxic-Heat) can heal within 1-3 weeks. Chronic, dry, itchy cracks from Blood Deficiency usually show less itching and softer skin in 2-4 weeks, with complete healing over a couple of months. Deeper patterns involving Cold or Spleen weakness take longer, often 3-6 months, but improvement is steady when you stick with the plan.

research.title: Chinese herbal medicine for atopic eczema: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials
research.description: This Cochrane-style systematic review evaluated multiple RCTs of Chinese herbal medicine for atopic eczema. It found that some herbal formulations improved eczema severity and reduced itching and skin lesions, but the evidence was weakened by poor trial design and small sample sizes.
research.periodical: Zhang W, Leonard T, Bath-Hextall F, Chambers CA, Lee C, Humphreys R, Williams HC. Chinese herbal medicine for atopic eczema: a systematic review of randomised controlled trials. British Journal of Dermatology. 2007;157(2):229-239.

research.title: Clinical observation on Dang Gui Yin Zi in treating chronic eczema of blood deficiency and wind-dryness type
research.description: This randomized controlled trial investigated the classic blood-nourishing formula Dang Gui Yin Zi in patients with chronic eczema presenting with dry, cracked, and itchy skin. The treatment group showed a significantly higher effective rate, with marked reduction in skin fissures, scaling, and pruritus compared to the control group.
research.periodical: Li X, Zhang Y, Wang J. Clinical observation on Dang Gui Yin Zi in treating chronic eczema of blood deficiency and wind-dryness type. Journal of Traditional Chinese Medicine. 2016;36(5):612-617.
